title: Sariputta's calm
hook: the wise one's verses: I don't long for death, I don't long for life (Theragatha, Sariputta)
carry: as a servant waits for wages

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kassapa's rocky hills, and his refrain that they delighted him. Your line was these hills delight me. Which place did you name out loud? Today, the wise one, and the way he waits. Day eight hundred four.

Payday. The work is already done. The money will come when it comes. A worker who's finished doesn't stand at the door all week waiting for it, and doesn't forget about it either. Sariputta, the disciple tradition remembers for his wisdom, reaches for that very picture in his verses. A hired worker, waiting for his wages. It's how he describes waiting for the end of his own life. Today, what that calm sounds like.
screen: `PAYDAY. THE WORK IS DONE.` → `SARIPUTTA, THE WISE ONE.` → `HOW HE WAITS.`

segments.voice: First, the two refusals. Sariputta says: I don't long for death. I don't long for life. Neither one pulls at him. He isn't hurrying toward the end, and he isn't clutching at more time. Second, the picture. I wait for my time, he says, as a servant waits for wages. And he adds something that matters: mindful, and clearly knowing. A hired worker who has finished the job isn't chasing the pay as a prize. It's simply what comes next. Sariputta's work, the long training of the mind, is complete. What's left is to wait, awake, without leaning either way. Third, the load. In his verses he says the teacher has been served, the heavy burden laid down, what leads to becoming rooted out. Other elders in the brothers' book close their songs with words like these. It's their way of saying: done. Fourth, why this can unsettle a listener. A line that won't long for life can sound bleak on first hearing. Read in his verses, it sounds closer to ease. He isn't tired of living. He just isn't grasping in either direction. Some readers hear in it the end of fear. Others hear a craftsman's quiet pride in finished work. Either way, the picture is plain: a worker at the end of the day, tools put away, sitting on the step until the pay arrives.
screen: `NO LONGING FOR DEATH, NOR FOR LIFE.` · `LIKE A WORKER WAITING FOR WAGES.` · `THE HEAVY BURDEN LAID DOWN.` · `NOT TIRED. NOT GRASPING.` · then, large: `AS A SERVANT WAITS FOR WAGES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait patiently for one thing. Choose something you're waiting on: a reply, a result, a season of life to end or to begin. Hold it in mind, then let go of the handle. You don't need to pull it closer or push it away. Sit the way a worker sits after the work is done: finished for now, not watching the door. Each time the mind leans toward the thing, lean back into the breath. The bell holds the time.
Sariputta's calm. The wise disciple's verses: no longing for death, no longing for life, waiting for his time, mindful, as a worker waits for wages. Today's word.
Your line: as a servant waits for wages. Today, when you catch yourself checking on something you're waiting for, set it down, and wait like that. Day eight hundred four.

howItsDone: Theravada teachers sometimes recite Sariputta's lines about not longing for death or life when speaking of how a freed person meets the end, and they are read at some reflections on death.

fork.setup: you're Sariputta. the work of training the mind is done, and the end of your life lies ahead. how do you meet it?
options: hold on to life for as long as you can.
wait for it, as a worker waits for wages.
fork.reveal: he longs for neither death nor life. he waits for his time, mindful and clearly knowing, like a hired worker waiting for his pay.

original.note: Pali: bhataka, a hired worker. Sariputta waits for his time as one waits for wages.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monk tired of living.
what it means: Sariputta's calm: he grasps at neither life nor death, and waits for his time like a worker for pay.
what a scholar hears: the verse joins the waiting to mindfulness and clear knowing, and his song speaks of the heavy burden laid down.
